angle: 10 employees with 10 audiences beat one founder with one. What I saw at Ramp
post_first_line: 10 people with audiences beat one founder.
linkedin_post:
10 people with audiences beat one founder.

That's what I learned watching how reach actually compounds.

If I have an audience, great. But if 10 people at our company each have their own independent audiences, the total reach is far bigger than anything I can get alone.

We see it most around fundraise announcements. We get the whole team posting their own unique stories, and we coach people on how to do it well. It makes a world of difference.

I saw the same thing at Ramp in 2020 and 2021. X was the big platform that worked there, and there was a lot of Twitter talk.

The people with the presence weren't just the founders. A bunch of the early hires on the team were the ones building it.

One founder voice has a ceiling. A team of voices, each with a different story and a different audience, doesn't.

Who on your team should be posting but isn't?

Slide 2: One founder's audience has a ceiling on reach.
Slide 3: Ten independent audiences add up to far more reach.
Slide 4: We get the whole team posting on fundraise announcements.
Slide 5: Each person tells their own unique story, not a copy.
Slide 6: We coach people on how to post effectively.
Slide 7: At Ramp in 2020, early hires built the presence.
Slide 8: Your team's voices are your biggest distribution channel.

lesson.title: Distribution is a team sport, not a founder sport
takeaways: Reach multiplies when many employees have their own independent audiences.
Big announcements like fundraises are the best moment to get the whole team posting.
At Ramp, early hires, not just founders, were key content creators on X.
lesson.exercise: Pick your next company announcement and ask 3 teammates to share their own take on it. Spend 15 minutes with each coaching them on their angle.

angle: The Dreamforce stunt drove fewer demos than the LinkedIn post about it
post_first_line: The Dreamforce stunt lost to its LinkedIn post.
linkedin_post:
The Dreamforce stunt lost to its LinkedIn post.

The post about it booked more demos than the stunt did, and not by a little.

We've done a few of these in real life. Most recently around the Super Bowl, with signs showing up in the background of First Take. Before that, the stunt at Dreamforce.

Sometimes the in-person moment works. We definitely have cases of that. Sometimes it doesn't.

But the stunt isn't the only asset. The social post you build from it can end up being the real campaign.

With AI lowering the barrier to entry for content, anyone can publish. Not everyone can do something in real life and then translate it into social.

Both of these also came organically from our team, which is part of why they were fun to do.

What's the last thing you did IRL that you turned into content?

Slide 8: Do something different, then translate it to social.

lesson.title: Treat the stunt as content, not just an event
takeaways: In-person stunts don't always work live, but the social post built from them can outperform the event itself.
As AI lowers the barrier to creating content, real-world moments become a way to stand out.
Ideas that come organically from your team are more fun to run and easier to turn into content.
lesson.exercise: Pick one small real-world thing your team could do this month, plan how you'll capture it, and draft the LinkedIn post before the event happens.

angle: The first LinkedIn post to write for any founder: your origin story
post_first_line: Origin story posts consistently top the charts.
linkedin_post:
Origin story posts consistently top the charts.

Tommy Clark sees the same pattern across every client Unify works with, and it's why this is always the first post to write.

People want to hear the story behind your company. It's a story only you can tell.

The format hits a few boxes at once:

It works as a milestone announcement, so people celebrate with you.

It humanizes you.

And if the founding story has conflict or an interesting turning point, it lands even harder. Tommy points out that almost every founder has one.

Austin has posted a few versions of this over time. An earlier one, and a newer one from just a couple weeks back. The format keeps working because the story keeps being worth telling.

If you're a founder who hasn't posted yours yet, start there.

What was the hardest moment in your founding story?

lesson.title: Start with your origin story
takeaways: Origin story posts are consistently among the best performing post types across Unify's clients.
People want the story behind the company, and only the founder can tell it.
The format combines a milestone announcement, humanization, and conflict that pulls readers in.
lesson.exercise: Write down the moment your company started, including the biggest conflict or surprise along the way. Turn it into a short LinkedIn post.

angle: The simple monthly update post: one metric, 3 wins, 3 learnings, what's next
post_first_line: Tommy Clark shared the simplest founder post to write.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark shared the simplest founder post to write.

It has one hook, three wins, three learnings, and a look ahead.

The monthly update starts with a growth metric or a big moment from the past month. Tommy's examples: a percentage you grew, a revenue milestone, a big logo you landed, or a few key hires.

The goal is something that catches attention on the timeline.

The more specific the metric, the better. Tommy pointed to Austin, who is comfortable sharing specific numbers, which is one reason these posts tend to work well for Austin.

After the hook, the structure is:

- 3 key highlights
- 3 learnings from the past month
- What's next

Tommy also pointed out that this is much easier to execute than an origin story post. There's no narrative through line to build. You share a highlight, list the wins, and say what you learned.

If you've been avoiding posting because you don't know what story to tell, a monthly update removes that excuse.

What metric would you lead with this month?

Slide 2: Lead with one growth metric or big moment from the month
Slide 3: A percentage grown, a revenue milestone, a big logo, key hires

Slide 5: Then share three key highlights from the past month
Slide 6: Follow with three learnings from the past month
Slide 7: Close with what's next
Slide 8: No narrative through line, so it beats an origin story post

lesson.title: The Simple Monthly Update Post
takeaways: Open with a specific growth metric or exciting event from the past month to catch attention on the timeline.
Structure the rest as three highlights, three learnings, and what's next.
It's easier than an origin story post because there's no narrative through line to build.
lesson.exercise: List your single most specific metric from the last 30 days, then write three wins, three learnings, and one line on what's next in under 15 minutes.

angle: LinkedIn content has asymmetric upside, but stop asking 'content or outbound' and stack both.
post_first_line: Tens of demos booked per month from content.
linkedin_post:
Tens of demos booked per month from content.

At Unify, that's what LinkedIn content has done for us. It's a standout case, so I wouldn't treat it as a guarantee. But the upside is asymmetric: if you're good at it, content can be the best-returning thing you do, and it doesn't take that much time.

Here's where I land: a pipeline strategy has to be multichannel. Asking "content or outbound?" is the wrong framing.

The better question is how you keep stacking multiple wins.

Outbound and outreach on LinkedIn is one win. Content on LinkedIn is another.

Stack them instead of picking one.

Which channel are you underinvesting in right now?
carousel: Slide 1: Content can book tens of demos a month.
Slide 2: It has asymmetric upside if you're actually good at it.
Slide 3: It also doesn't take that much time.
Slide 4: At Unify, that's been our own lived experience.
Slide 5: But it's a standout case, not a guarantee.
Slide 6: Stop asking: content or outbound?
Slide 7: Ask how you keep stacking multiple wins.
Slide 8: Outbound on LinkedIn plus content on LinkedIn. Run both.

lesson.title: Stack channels instead of choosing one
takeaways: Content has asymmetric upside: if you're good, it can be your best-returning channel, with tens-plus demos booked per month.
Content's results are a standout case, so don't rely on it alone.
A multichannel pipeline strategy beats either/or thinking. Outbound and content on LinkedIn are separate wins to stack.
lesson.exercise: List every channel you use to generate pipeline. Mark which ones you run consistently, then pick one missing channel (content or outbound) and commit to running it alongside the others for 30 days.

angle: AI made posting easy. Here's why that makes your stories the only thing worth posting
post_first_line: Tommy Clark says AI killed how-to content.
linkedin_post:
Tommy Clark says AI killed how-to content.

Here's what replaces it.

It's easy to toss a prompt into Claude or ChatGPT and get a pretty okay piece of LinkedIn copy. The barrier to posting has dropped, and the timeline is getting more crowded.

Tommy's advice is to find specific ways to stand out and create content AI can't copy.

One of the best: shift from how-to content to first-person story content. Add more narrative and story to what gets published.

The rule Tommy uses is simple: pair every take with a story.

A take on its own is something a model can generate in seconds. A story from real work is not.

What's the last story you turned into a post?

Slide 2: Anyone can prompt a pretty okay post in seconds.
Slide 3: The timeline is getting more crowded every week.
Slide 4: Standing out means creating content AI can't copy.
Slide 5: Shift from how-to content to how-I content.
Slide 6: Add more narrative and stories to your posts.

Slide 8: Takes are easy to copy. Your stories are not.

lesson.title: Pair every take with a story
takeaways: AI has lowered the barrier to posting, so the timeline is more crowded and generic copy blends in.
Shifting from how-to content to how-I content makes your posts harder for AI to copy.
A simple rule: pair every single take with a story.
lesson.exercise: Pick your next post idea and write down the take in one sentence. Then add one story from your own work that shows it in action, and lead with the story.
